message.content:
Below is a concise summary of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is not legal advice; if you need help with a specific situation, consider contacting a local attorney or tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months’ rent for an unfurnished unit. | Keep a written receipt when you pay the deposit. Ask for a written itemized list of any deductions before you move out. | | **Notice Requirements** | • 30‑day notice for month‑to‑month leases.
• 60‑day notice if the lease term is longer than 12 months. | Get the notice in writing and keep a copy. If you receive a notice that seems shorter than required, you may contest it. | | **Habitability** | Landlords must maintain the premises in a safe, sanitary condition—plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control, etc. | Document problems (photos, emails). Give the landlord written notice and allow reasonable time to fix issues. | | **Rent Payment** | Rent is due on the date specified in the lease. Late fees are allowed but cannot exceed 10% of the monthly rent. | Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Entry Rights** | Landlords must give at least 24 hours written notice before entering, except in emergencies. | Keep a log of all entries. If the landlord enters without notice, you can file a complaint. | | **Discrimination** | Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, family status, or source of income. | Report any discriminatory behavior to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or your local fair‑housing agency. | | **Eviction Process** | Evictions require a court order. The landlord must serve a written notice (usually 3 days for nonpayment, 30 days for lease violations). You have the right to contest the eviction in court. | Respond promptly to notices. If you receive a notice, you can file a “Notice to Quit” defense or request a hearing. | | **Lease Termination** | Either party can terminate a month‑to‑month lease with proper notice. For fixed‑term leases, you may break the lease only under certain circumstances (e.g., landlord fails to maintain the property). | Review your lease for any “break‑lease” clauses. If you need to leave early, discuss options with your landlord (subletting, lease transfer). | | **Legal Assistance** | Texas has several nonprofit tenant‑advocacy groups and legal aid clinics. | Contact the Texas Tenants Association, Legal Aid of North Texas, or your local county bar association for free or low‑cost help. | ### Quick Checklist Before Moving In 1. **Get a written lease** – read it carefully; ask questions about any clause you don’t understand. 2. **Document the condition** – take photos or video of the unit before you move in. 3. **Ask for a copy of the lease** – keep a signed copy for your records. 4. **Know your local ordinances** – some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas) have additional tenant protections beyond state law. ### When Things Go Wrong - **Write everything down** – keep copies of emails, texts, and a written log of incidents. - **Give written notice** – send a certified letter or email to prove delivery. - **File a complaint** – you can file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office or HUD if you suspect unlawful practices. --- If you’d like a sample lease or a more detailed contract tailored to your situation, let me know and I can generate one for you.
